title: "Day 06: Transforming SLR models"

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(ggformula)
library(broom)
library(patchwork)
library(mosaic)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

redcedar <- read.csv("https://github.com/math430-lu/data/raw/master/ufcwc.csv")
data("case0802", package = "Sleuth3")

redcedar_mod <- lm(Height ~ Dbh, data = redcedar)
aug_cedar <- augment(redcedar_mod)
```

## Last time

We checked: are any conditions for SLR *violated*? Is there a strong
predictive relationship between X and Y? **Today:** how can we fix the
worst violation?

If the linearity condition is not met, we get systematically biased
predictions, might draw false conclusions about the existence or
strength of a relationship, and all inference about
$\beta_0, \beta_1, \widehat\mu(Y \mid X), \mathrm{Pred}(Y \mid X)$
becomes meaningless.

## Easing skew

If a set of data values is skewed to the right, taking the (natural)
log of each value *can* result in a data set that is roughly symmetric
and often roughly normal.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 8
h1 <- gf_histogram(~Time, data = case0802, fill = "#003300", col = "white")
qq1 <- gf_qq(~Time, data = case0802, color = "#003300") %>% gf_qqline()
h2 <- gf_histogram(~log(Time), data = case0802, fill = "#003300", col = "white")
qq2 <- gf_qq(~log(Time), data = case0802, color = "#003300") %>% gf_qqline()
(h1 +  qq1 + h2 + qq2) + plot_layout(ncol = 4)
```

**New Data for today**: Red Cedar

How are tree height and tree diameter related for the western red
cedar?

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 8
p_scat <- gf_point(Height ~ Dbh, data = redcedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_lm(color = "#f15a31") %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Diameter (mm)", y = "Height (dm)")

p_resid <- gf_point(.resid ~ Dbh, data = aug_cedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Diameter", y = "Residuals")

p_qq <- gf_qq(~.resid, data = aug_cedar, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_qqline() %>%
  gf_labs(x = "N(0, 1) quantiles", y = "Residuals")

(p_scat | p_resid | p_qq)
```

Which condition(s) look violated here: (a) linearity (b) independent
errors (c) normal errors (d) equal variance (e) outliers (f) none? 
**Answer:** ___________________________

Adding `gf_smooth()` to the residual plot can help reveal curvature,
but trust your eyes first, and don't over-interpret small samples.

**Does transforming X help?**

Answer:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 8
logx_mod <- lm(Height ~ log(Dbh), data = redcedar)
aug <- augment(logx_mod)
xlab <- "Diameter (mm) (log scale)"; ylab <- "Height (dm)"

p1 <- gf_point(Height ~ log(Dbh), data = redcedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_lm(color = "#f15a31") %>% gf_labs(x = xlab, y = ylab)
p2 <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2) %>% gf_labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Std. residuals")
p3 <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_qqline() %>% gf_labs(x = "N(0, 1) quantiles", y = "Std. residuals")
(p1 | p2 | p3)
```

**Does transforming Y help?**

Answer:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 8
logy_mod <- lm(log(Height) ~ Dbh, data = redcedar)
aug <- augment(logy_mod)
xlab <- "Diameter (mm)"; ylab <- "Height (log scale)"

p1 <- gf_point(log(Height) ~ Dbh, data = redcedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_lm(color = "#f15a31") %>% gf_labs(x = xlab, y = ylab)
p2 <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2) %>% gf_labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Std. residuals")
p3 <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_qqline() %>% gf_labs(x = "N(0, 1) quantiles", y = "Std. residuals")
(p1 | p2 | p3)
```

**Transforming both X and Y?**

Answer:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 8
logxy_mod <- lm(log(Height) ~ log(Dbh), data = redcedar)
aug <- augment(logxy_mod)
xlab <- "Diameter (log scale)"; ylab <- "Height (log scale)"

p1 <- gf_point(log(Height) ~ log(Dbh), data = redcedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_lm(color = "#f15a31") %>% gf_labs(x = xlab, y = ylab)
p2 <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2) %>% gf_labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Std. residuals")
p3 <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_qqline() %>% gf_labs(x = "N(0, 1) quantiles", y = "Std. residuals")
(p1 | p2 | p3)
```

# Back-transforming

Converting a transformed variable back to its original scale.

## Example: back-transforming a mean

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 4
gf_histogram(~log(Time), data = case0802, fill = "#003300", col = "white")
```

```{r}
mean_logtime <- mean(log(case0802$Time))
```

Mean of `log(Time)` = `r round(mean_logtime, 3)`.

Back-transformed mean: $e^{`r round(mean_logtime, 3)`} \approx$ `r round(exp(mean_logtime), 2)`.

Original `mean(Time)` = `r round(mean(case0802$Time), 3)`

::: {.callout-note}
## Note

`log()` is the *natural* log; `exp(x)` calculates $e^x$. **Note:**
back-transforming the mean of the logs does **not** generally equal
the mean on the original scale, but estimates the median instead.
:::

## Displaying a transformed model

`gf_lm(formula = log(y) ~ log(x), backtrans = exp, interval = "confidence")`
plots the fitted line and CI back-transformed onto the *original*
scale, so you can show results in units your audience understands.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 8
left <- gf_point(log(Height) ~ log(Dbh), data = redcedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_lm(interval = "confidence", color = "#f15a31") %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Diameter (mm) (log scale)", y = "Height (dm) (log scale)", title = "Transformed scale")

right <- gf_point(Height ~ Dbh, data = redcedar, alpha = 0.5, color = "#003300") %>%
  gf_lm(formula = log(y) ~ log(x), backtrans = exp, interval = "confidence", color = "#f15a31") %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Diameter (mm)", y = "Height (dm)", title = "Original scale")

left + right
```

## Rules of thumb

-   **Transform X:** if the mean function is nonlinear, but
    monotonic, and the residual variance is constant.
-   **Transform Y:** if the mean function is nonlinear *and* residual
    variance increases as the mean increases (log, reciprocal, or
    square root often work).
-   **Log rule:** if values range over more than 1 order of magnitude
    and are strictly positive, the natural log is likely helpful.
-   **Range rule:** if the range is considerably less than 1 order of
    magnitude, transformations are unlikely to help.
-   **Square roots** are useful for count data.

## Ladder of transformations & Rule of the Bulge

Tukey and Mosteller's "Rule of the Bulge" gives a visual guide: match
the direction your scatterplot bulges to the ladder position, and
move X and/or Y toward that end to straighten the relationship.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| layout-ncol: 2
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("slides", "img", "clipboard-2725667272.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("slides", "img", "clipboard-2203698702.png"))
```

## Issues with transformations

-   You're often guessing -- statistics is an art *and* a science.
-   Transformations change the ___________________________ of the
    parameters -- you need to back-transform to give interpretable
    results.
-   Transformations change the SEs of the parameters.
-   Not always easy to keep track of all your assumptions once you've
    transformed.
